title: Flame Tests

stepCard.title: Step card
steps: Dip a fresh splint in one salt. Hold it at the edge of the flame for 10 seconds.
Record the color and the brightness.
Test all six salts and NaNO3 (the control).
Take unknown bottles A and B. Test them.
If two knowns match, use the spectroscope.
Write your claim, evidence and reasoning.

tutorial2: The spectroscope splits flame light into its colors.
Each line is one color the metal gives out.
Same crimson to the eye, different lines.
specGuide: Each black row is what a spectroscope shows for one metal. Each bright line is one color of light that metal gives out, placed at its wavelength; the strip on top shows which color sits where. Look first at where the lines fall, then compare with the other rows. Sr has a blue line near 461 nm; Li has none. That separates the two crimson metals. Wrong reading: a taller or thicker line does not tell you how bright the flame looked. The faint glow behind Sr and Cu is a wide band. The two K lines at the far right are at the edge of vision.
swatchGuide: Each box is the flame color you will see, with its name underneath. Look first at the two Na boxes: they match on purpose. Watch for Li and Sr: those two boxes are identical too, and that is the problem the lab ends on.
intro: Today you test salts in a flame and name two unknowns from the colors.
introSteps: Do the pre-lab: three pictures and one prediction. The lab door stays shut until you finish.
Huddle 1: Mr. D gives you the first code.
Suit up, go to the flame bench, and follow the step card.
Test six salts and NaNO3, then unknown bottles A and B.
Write your claim, evidence and reasoning. Huddle 2 comes after your data.
keyRows: Use what you are facing (locker, shelf, bench, door).
Step away from the bench, or close a window.
Point at anything to see its name.

h1.title: Huddle 1 (minute 3, about 8 min)
script: Review (3 min): the three pre-lab items and the prediction. Do not give the prediction away.
First contact (4 min): a flame test puts a pinch of a salt in a flame, and you watch the color.
Say the three rules: known salts first, a fresh splint each time, and record everything in the notebook.
Say: if two flames look the same, there is a second tool on the bench (the spectroscope).
Show the swatches so no color name arrives unexplained. Look first at the two Na boxes: they match on purpose. Watch for Li and Sr: identical too, and that is the problem the lab ends on.

h2.title: Huddle 2 (about minute 33, 6 min)
h2.picture: Three energy levels as horizontal lines, an electron dot on level 3, a long straight arrow down to level 1 with a wavy blue arrow (bluer light), a short arrow down to level 2 with a wavy red arrow (redder light). The straight arrow is a drop between two energies, not a path through space.
definitions: a specific energy an electron can have
light given off when an electron drops to a lower level
metal, not the other part of the salt

worked.problem: NaCl and NaNO3 both burn yellow-orange.
worked.say: Claim: the metal sets the color. Evidence: two different salts, one color. Reasoning: the only part they share is sodium.

worked.problem: A flame flashes yellow, then shows lilac.
worked.say: Claim: potassium, with a little sodium on the splint. Evidence: the color that lasts is lilac. Reasoning: sodium is very bright and can hide a faint color.

worked.problem: An unknown burns crimson; Li and Sr are both crimson.
worked.say: Claim first: I cannot tell from the flame alone, both match. PAUSE: students say how the spectroscope settled it (the blue line). Then say: an honest answer says what the data cannot decide. That is part of the evidence.

crux.q: Picture: an electron dropping between two levels. What comes out?
Picture: two flames, same color, labeled NaCl and NaNO3. What sets the color?
Table: an unknown is crimson. Write a claim true to the data.
crux.answer: Li or Sr; a second test is needed
crux.expect: Li, because it is listed first

h2.note: Give code 2 at the end. Code 2 only works on a student whose record is complete (seven flame tests recorded, both unknowns answered). In creative mode the code is shown instead.
